newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD wants to spread influence but not ranks.
newsitem.headline: OECD wants to spread influence but not ranks.

text.p: The OECD said on Tuesday it wanted closer ties with countries which aspired to its free-market ideology, but made it clear membership was a faraway prospect for Russia and others.

The Organisation for Co-Operation and Development, whose membership has swelled to 29 with the entry of several former Soviet bloc countries in recent years, signed a new cooperation deal with Russia.

It steered clear, however, of any promise to accept Russia's request to join, limiting itself to saying that membership was the "ultimate goal shared by both parties" and that it hoped the stronger cooperation would help Russia develop a fully fledged market economy there.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, who chaired the OECD's two-day ministerial summit here, told a news conference he hoped Slovakia would soon complete long-running membership talks and that "caution" would apply on further expansion of OECD ranks.

The OECD, which was celebrating its creation 50 years ago to channel $13 billion of U.S. Marshall Plan aid to western Europe after World War II, has recently shed some of the rich country-club image that it acquired over the decades.

With the trend towards an increasingly international economy which it actively supports, and the emergence of new fast-growing economies, the OECD has in recent years allowed Mexico and South Korea to join the fold along with ex-Soviet bloc states like Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland.

But it has come under increasing pressure to streamline, cut back on costs and work which overlaps with other international bodies, as governments in its member countries tighten the screws on public spending and on OECD funding as a result.

Within the OECD, the debate is still raging on whether and how fast it should expand and whether the OECD can spread its free-market gospel in developing countries without swelling its own ranks to an unwieldy size.

On the sidelines of the meeting, European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan tried but failed to hammer out a deal with U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky to eliminate red tape in trade between the European Union and the United States.

Brittan had hoped to overcome U.S. resistance to a "mutual recognition agreement" so that pharmaceutical, medical devices, telecoms, electrical and other products which have got safety approval in the European Union would not need double-checks before entering the United States and vice-versa.

U.S. officials said differences had been narrowed but that chances of a quick deal were slim. EU officials said they still hoped a deal might be struck on Wednesday to coincide with a meeting between U.S. President Bill Clinton and European Commission President Jacques Santer.
An agreement across all the sectors concerned would cover trade in products worth an estimated $40 billion, according to U.S. estimates, an EU official said.

The trouble spots are pharmaceutical products and medical devices, where the powerful U.S. Food and Drug Administration is reluctant to lose the power to keep tabs and carry out spot checks on EU safety approval agencies, officials said.
The OECD summit, which gathered a mixture of finance, trade, social and foreign affairs ministers, issued its now traditional message of confidence in the "globalisation" of the economy.
But it tempered its words, at a time of mass unemployment in many member countries, to say that the benefits of international trade should be shared with the poor and marginalised.
The co-operation pact with Russia, which includes setting up twice-yearly meetings at a high level, was signed by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
